Maladaptive Strategies.value: I pretend it happened to someone else
ruminate about how event could have been prevented
avoid anything that could be stressful

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

issues.explanation: These items form a combat/interpersonal-violence style hypervigilance pattern centered on armed human threat, which is hard to reconcile with a natural-disaster trauma. A disaster survivor may be generally vigilant, but carrying a weapon and scanning for weapons specifically are not a coherent extension of the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
issues.explanation: The threat profile is narrowly organized around deliberate human attack (weapons, tactical positioning), while the memory items are generic intrusion/detachment phenomena and do not support that specific threat theme. This creates a cross-node mismatch rather than a plausible disaster-related PTSD presentation.

vignette:
Gerald Mauer is a 74-year-old man of German descent who lives with his long-term partner in a mid-sized town in the Pacific Northwest. He works part-time as a private tutor, primarily helping high school students with mathematics and German language, a role he has held since retiring from secondary school teaching nearly a decade ago. He presented for psychological assessment following what he described, with considerable understatement, as "a rough couple of years."

Approximately eighteen months ago, Gerald was at his partner's lakeside cabin in a rural area when a fast-moving wildfire swept through the surrounding hillside. The fire had been reported several miles away the previous evening, and emergency services had not yet issued an evacuation order for the cabin's zone. Gerald was alone that afternoon - his partner had driven into town for supplies - when the wind shifted and the fire crested the ridge above the property within minutes. He had no time to gather belongings. The air turned a dense, acrid orange, and the smell of burning pine and char filled the cabin before he even opened the door. He drove out along a single-lane road with flames visible on both sides, unable to see more than a few metres ahead through the smoke, certain at several points that he would not make it. The cabin was destroyed. Gerald was physically unharmed, but he did not speak to anyone about what had happened for several weeks.

In the months that followed, the memory of that afternoon began to intrude on Gerald's life in ways he found deeply unsettling. The memory did not arrive when he invited it; it arrived without warning, forcing itself into his awareness during tutoring sessions, during meals, during the quiet of early morning. When it came, it sometimes brought with it the smell - that particular combination of burning resin and hot ash - as though the fire were still present in the room. At other times, he found he could revisit the events in a flat, detached way, recounting what had happened to his partner as though describing a film he had once seen, the words accurate but emptied of any feeling he could recognise as his own. He had come to think of this as a kind of mercy, though it also disturbed him, because he was certain the man on that road had been terrified, and he could not always locate that terror in himself.

Gerald began to restructure his days around the avoidance of anything that felt unpredictable or potentially stressful. He declined tutoring students who struck him as difficult or whose parents seemed demanding. He stopped accepting new clients entirely by the autumn, reducing his working hours to a handful of familiar students. When one of his remaining students failed to arrive at the scheduled time, Gerald would sit rigidly at the table, convinced that something had gone wrong - an accident, a crisis - his mind moving immediately toward catastrophe. The same response came in other contexts: a delayed text from his partner, a slow internet connection, a package that had not arrived. Any gap between expectation and reality had become, in his experience, a signal that something bad was unfolding.

In public spaces - a café, a waiting room, a library - Gerald found he could not settle unless he could position himself with his back to a wall and a clear view of the exits and other occupants. He scanned every environment he entered, cataloguing faces and doorways, tracking movement. He was aware this looked odd, and he had begun to avoid social engagements partly for this reason, which had placed a quiet strain on his relationship. His partner had noticed the withdrawal, the shortened temper when routines were disrupted, and had gently encouraged him to seek help.

Gerald also spent considerable time turning the events of that afternoon over in his mind, returning again and again to the moments before the fire crested the ridge - the weather reports he had read, the decision to stay, the window of time in which he might have left sooner. He was not sure he could have known, but he was equally not sure he could not have. This uncertainty had become its own kind of occupation.

What finally brought Gerald to the clinic was a session with a student in which he smelled, briefly and unmistakably, the smoke from a neighbour's fireplace drifting through the window - and found himself unable to continue for several minutes. He was embarrassed by this, and frightened by it. What he hoped for, he said quietly, was to feel like himself again. What he feared was that the man he had been before that afternoon no longer existed.
